title: Variables and data types
objective: Create variables with let and const and get to know text, number and boolean values
story: The rocket's control panel has dozens of gauges: fuel, speed, the pilot's name... We need to store each of them somewhere. Today we put information into labeled boxes: **variables**.

sections.title: A variable is a labeled box
sections.body:
A variable lets you store a value under a name. You create the box with `let` and put a value into it with `=`:

```js
let fuel = 100;
console.log(fuel);   // 100
fuel = 80;           // change the value
console.log(fuel);   // 80
```

When you change the value you don't write `let` again; `let` is only used when you first create the box.

sections.title: let or const?
sections.body:
- `let`: for boxes whose value **will change** (fuel, score).
- `const`: for boxes whose value **never changes** (the rocket's name, the game's rules).

```js
const shipName = "Eagle-1";
shipName = "Falcon";  // Error! a const can't be changed
```

In older code you may see `var`; today `let` and `const` are used instead.

sections.title: Data types
sections.body:
Every value in JavaScript has a type. Today, three basic types:

- **string** (text): `"Mars"`, `'Moon'`
- **number**: `42`, `3.14`, `-7`
- **boolean**: `true` or `false`

`typeof` tells you a value's type: `typeof "Mars"` gives `"string"`, `typeof 42` gives `"number"`.

Careful: `"7"` is text, `7` is a number. Quotes change everything!

sections.title: Naming rules
sections.body:
- A name starts with a letter, `_` or `$`; it can't start with a digit: `ship2` works, `2ship` doesn't.
- No spaces. Several words are written in **camelCase**: `pilotName`, `fuelLevel`.
- Upper and lower case matter: `fuel` and `Fuel` are two different variables.
- Choose names that say what's inside: `fuel` instead of `x`.

examples.title: Rocket card
examples.note: fuel = fuel - 20: take 20 away from the old value and put the result back into fuel.

tasks.title: Pilot card
tasks.prompt:
Create your own pilot card:

- Create a **const** called `pilotName` and put your name in it (text).
- Create a **let** called `age` and put your age in it (a number, no quotes).
- Print both with `console.log(pilotName, age);`
tasks.starter:
// Create the pilotName and age variables

console.log(pilotName, age);
hints: Age is a number: let age = 12; (no quotes)

tasks.title: Fuel used
tasks.prompt:
The rocket used 35 liters of fuel at launch.

- Subtract 35 from the `fuel` variable (and put the result back into `fuel`). Don't type the number 65 yourself!
- Then print `Fuel left: 65`.
hints: The new value is calculated from the old one: fuel = fuel - ...

tasks.title: Type detective
tasks.prompt: Print the type of the three variables in order with `typeof`. The output should be three lines: `number`, `string`, `boolean`.
hints: You can write three separate console.log lines.

challenge.title: Swap places
challenge.prompt:
**Swap** the values of the `left` and `right` variables: in the end `left` should be "Mars" and `right` "Moon".

Rule: don't type the texts `"Mars"` and `"Moon"` a second time. A third variable can help.
hints: To swap the water in two glasses you need a third glass.
const temp = left; then left = right; finally right = temp;

project_task.title: Player data
project_task.prompt:
Let's keep the game's data in variables:

- `shipName`: the ship's name (**const**, any name you like)
- `stars`: stars collected, starting at `0` (**let**)
- `lives`: lives, starting at `3` (**let**)

Then print the status with the ready-made line. Example output: `Ship: Eagle | Stars: 0 | Lives: 3`
project_task.starter:
// Create the shipName, stars and lives variables

console.log("Ship:", shipName, "| Stars:", stars, "| Lives:", lives);
hints: The name won't change: const shipName = "...";
The ones that change use let: let stars = 0;
